title: LOUISVILLE VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Louisville Village Board met Tuesday night after postponing last Thursday’s regular meeting.

Mayor Chris Rinehart opened the session and invited public comments. With no visitors present, the board quickly approved the agenda, past meeting minutes, and the bills — all without opposition.

Rinehart then updated trustees on a proposed rate increase from Utility Gas Management. The supplier wants to raise the natural gas rate from five cents to nine cents per MMBTU. After a brief discussion, the board approved the UGM amendment.

Trustees also approved training for Village Clerk Leah Stine. She plans to attend the Municipal Clerks of Illinois Institute and Master Academy in Bloomington from October 4th through the 9th.

During open discussion, Trustee Tim Davis said he was glad to see the car wash open again. Other members agreed. Davis also reported talking with the Genealogical Society about protecting their building for the future.

The mayor noted that work on the K-1 building is finished and said he would like to see new flooring replace some of the existing tile.

Board members also discussed the village weather sirens and the possibility of Clay County ESDA taking over responsibility for activating them during severe weather. Rinehart said talks will continue, though some upgrades are still needed.

Finally, the mayor announced a meeting set for September 21st at 6 p.m. with Jamie Stang Ellis of Effingham to discuss creating a mural on the courthouse square or another location in Louisville.

Members also talked about improving the appearance of the lights around the square.

title: DRIVE THRU FLU SHOT CLINIC
full_story:
The Clay County Health Department has released their schedule for drive thru Flu shot clinics.  The First will be today from 9 am to 4 pm at the Health Department.  People wanting flu shots should follow the signs to the carport, no appointment is needed.  Please bring your Medicare Part B Card, HMO Card, Medicaid Card, or insurance card.  If uninsured, underinsured, or insurance is out of network, you may be charged a small administration fee.

There will also be drive through clinics on September 23rd, September 30th, October 7th, October 14th, October 21st and October 28th at the Health Department, from 9 to 4.

The Health Department will also be administering flu shots at the Xenia Community Center on October 7th from 11:30 to 12:30, at the Ingraham Bank on October 8th from 9 to 10 am, at the Louisville Farm Bureau October 13th from 10:15 to 11:15, at the Clay City Bank on October 16th from 9 to 10 am.

The Health Department says getting the flu vaccine is the best way to protect yourself, your family, and your community from the flu.  The Health Department will be administering the trivalent flu vaccine or the higher dose influenza vaccinations.  Different flu strains circulate every flu season, making it important that you get an annual flu shot.

title: SANTA SMILES APPLICATIONS
full_story:
Applications for Santa Smiles for this year will be available October 1st.

Applications can be picked up at the Clay City Village Hall, Xenia Village Hall, Louisville Village Hall, Louisville Banking Company, or Salt & Strings Butchery.  In Flora applications are available at the Flora City Hall, Flora Library, CEFS, and the office of Todd Fender at the Clay County Housing Authority.  The Clay County Health Department will give their applications to their clients.

Applications are due on November 1st and can be dropped off at the Clay City Village Hall, Louisville Village Hall, and Xenia City Hall.  In Flora Applications can be dropped off at the Clay County Housing authority night drop box.  Applications can also be mailed.

Santa Smiles will also have a Christmas Auction on Friday, October 23rd at 6 pm at the Xenia Community Center.  Santa Smiles is providing concessions at the auction.

Again, applications will be available on October 1st.  Last year Santa Smiles provided gifts to 523 kids, and 71 residents at Chestnut Corner Sheltered Care in Louisville.

Andi Malone will be the guest today on the ReVue talking about Santa Smiles.

title: NORTH WAYNE PRESCHOOL SCREENINGS
full_story:
The North Wayne Schools are conducting Child Find/Preschool Screenings for children who are 3 to 5-years in age, not yet enrolled in public schools and who will not be Kindergarten eligible in the fall.  Child/Find screenings check each child’s progress in hearing, vision, speech, and other developmental areas.  This screening program is free, and parents will receive immediate feedback on how their child is developing.

The Child Find/Preschool Screening will be held at Johnsonville School on Monday.  Appointments are necessary for this free service.

Child Find/Preschool Screening enables you to gain valuable knowledge concerning your child’s development.  The screening procedure takes about 45 minutes, and appointments must be made so that children don’t have a long wait period.  Parents should call 618-673-3044 to make an appointment or to get more information.

The service is a free check of your child’s progress in the development areas, but appointments are needed.  If you live in the North Wayne School District call 618-673-3044 today to make an appointment for your preschooler.

The following items are required for the screening, proof of income, W2 or 2 consecutive pay stubs, and a certified copy of your child’s birth certificate from the courthouse.

title: IPRB SCHOLARSHIPS
full_story:
The Illinois Petroleum Resource Board announced the co-recipients of the 2026 IPRB Post-Secondary Education Oil and Gas Scholarship.  The scholarship is funded by the registration fees from the annual math and science teachers summer program.

In our area Callista Ridgely a 2026 graduate of Richland County High School is a winner.  Callista is attending Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology where she is majoring in chemical engineering.  She has job shadowed at the Marathon refinery in Robinson and the CountryMark refinery in Mt. Vernon, Ind. and has always been fascinated by energy.

Also, Brody Runyon a 2024 graduate of Richland County High School, was awarded a scholarship.  Brody is entering his junior year at Oklahoma University where he is majoring in Energy Management.  Brody completed a landman internship at Mewborne Oil Company this summer.  Brody plans to pursue a career in land management in the Illinois Basin after he graduates from Oklahoma University.

The Scholarships are available to Illinois residents pursuing oil and gas related college degrees or trade and technical school certification, and can be up to $5,000.

title: ISP ACE PATROLS
full_story:
Illinois State Police Troop 9 Commander, Bruce Waggoner, announced that the ISP will be conducting Alcohol Countermeasure Enforcement (ACE) Patrols in Clay, Marion, Effingham, Wayne Lawrence, and White Counties during October.  Ace patrols allow the ISP to focus on preventing, detecting, and taking enforcement action in response to violations associated with impaired driving and illegal transportation or consumption of alcohol or drugs.

The ISP has zero tolerance for impaired driving in Illinois. Officers working the detail will be watchful for motorists who show signs of impaired driving, operating vehicles in an unsafe manner, driving with a suspended or revoked driver’s license, and transporting open alcoholic beverages, as well as improper seatbelt and child restraint usage, distracted driving, and other Illinois Vehicle Code violations.

Alcohol and drug impairment are estimated to be a factor in more than 47% of all fatal motor vehicle crashes in Illinois.  There is one alcohol-related traffic fatality every 39 minutes in the United States.  The ACE program allows officers to work even harder at removing dangerous DUI offenders from the road.  This project is funded through the Illinois Department of Transportation.

title: LAKE LAND ENROLLMENT NUMBERS
full_story:
Enrollment at Lake Land College reached a new seven-year high, according to the College’s Fall 2026 Census Day Enrollment Report, which was presented to the Board of Trustees during the regular September meeting.

According to the report, 4,313 students are enrolled at Lake Land College for the Fall 2026 semester, surpassing last year’s headcount by more than 4%.  Additionally, the report includes a 1.8% increase in Full-Time Equivalent (FTE) enrollment, which is the number of total enrolled credit hours divided by the conventional full-time workload of 15 credit hours per semester.  For the Fall 2026 semester, FTE at Lake Land College reached 2,611.3, the highest level since 2019.

Lake Land College President Josh Bullock also noted that Lake Land’s Fall 2026 enrollment is boosted by a strong retention rate, highlighted in the report by a 3.7% increase in the number of continuing students.

Lake Land’s increasing enrollment also points to strong momentum from the College’s ongoing strategic plan, Education that Fits Your Life, which prioritizes flexible, accessible options for students of all ages and backgrounds.  For the Fall 2026 semester, enrollment for students above the age of 23 reached a total of 895, surpassing last year’s count by 6.2%.  Additionally, part-time enrollment saw a substantial increase in demand for Fall 2026, rising 8.9% over the previous year and accounting for roughly 60% of total student headcount.  The increases in these enrollment areas coincide with the introduction of flexible new programs for the Fall semester, including an innovative Competency-Based Education model, which helps students balance their education with work, family and other commitments.

Additional highlights from the report include a 10% increase in headcount and an 11% increase in FTE for high school dual credit enrollment, which totals 1,500 for the Fall 2026 semester.  The increase points to continued success from the College’s Laker Connect Dual Credit program, which was recently introduced to strengthen partnerships among area high schools and increase access to higher education.  Since the introduction of Laker Connect in Fall 2024, dual credit enrollment has increased by 28.7%, helping more high school students than ever explore career paths, complete college-level credentials and build momentum toward higher education.

Lake Land’s Census Day numbers also point to the College’s strong outreach and connection throughout the many communities within its district, the second largest geographically among all Illinois community colleges.  For Fall 2026, roughly 30% of all high school graduates within the district enrolled at Lake Land College, an impressive figure that comes at a time when nearly half of all local high school graduates forgo college altogether.  Among these district high schools, 13 of them saw at least 35% of their graduating seniors choose Lake Land College including North Clay Community High School 40%, Dieterich Community High School 45.9%, and Effingham High School 40.8%.

The Census Day Enrollment Report, finalized on the 10th instructional day of the Fall term, is a standard report among the higher education community that captures opening enrollment data each semester.

title: BALLOON FEST MOVES
full_story:
The Centralia City Council approved an ordinance permitting the Centralia Chamber of Commerce to host Balloon Fest annually at Fairview Park.  The Chamber relocated the event to Fairview Park this year claiming that an understanding with the Centralia Foundation could not be reached about electrical improvements needed in Foundation Park.  Chamber director Marcus Holland said at Monday’s meeting that following a successful Balloon Fest in Fairview Park this year, the board voted to make it the event’s home for the foreseeable future.

Holland says the Chamber has invested in Fairview Park with the hope of improving Balloon Fest and other events being held in the park in the future.

Holland said that Balloon Fest in Fairview Park had the highest total attendance in recent years.  The Chamber estimates that 30,000 people attended this year’s Balloon Fest, while average attendance in Foundation Park was around 20,000.

title: MAIL IN VOTING
full_story:
The US Supreme Court issued an order late Monday blocking the Trump administration from implementing new rules that would have allowed the Postal Service to block certain people from casting mail-in ballots in the upcoming midterm elections.

In a 7-2 ruling, the justices let stand a lower court order blocking the Postal Service from implementing the rules, saying the government was “unlikely to succeed on the merits” of its appeal.

“The court’s decision is a victory for voters, for democracy, and for the rule of law in this country,” Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said in a statement.  “I am pleased that the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court’s decisions to stop this un-American rule from taking effect and creating chaos before the midterm election.”

The rules in question would have given the Postal Service broad authority to regulate balloting by mail nationwide.  They would have required all mail ballot envelopes to conform with uniform standards.  They also would have prohibited mail carriers from transmitting ballots to or from any person not listed on a federally approved list of confirmed US citizens eligible to vote.

Raoul was among a coalition of Democratic attorneys general who filed a lawsuit challenging the rules.  In August, a federal judge in Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction blocking the rules, but the Supreme Court overturned that injunction on procedural grounds because the Postal Service had not yet finalized the rules.

Once the rules were finalized, the same Massachusetts judge issued another injunction blocking them from going into effect while the legal challenge made its way through the courts.  The Trump administration appealed that ruling, but in an emergency order issued late Monday, the court let the new injunction stand.

The decision came just 10 days before mail-in voting and early in-person voting begins in Illinois, and seven weeks before Election Day on November 3rd.

David Becker, an election law expert and executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, said the court’s decision prevented the upcoming election from devolving into chaos.

“These rules would have done nothing for election integrity but would have imposed a vast and expensive new bureaucracy on the states, given massive new responsibilities to a Postal Service already overwhelmed by its current core responsibilities, and disenfranchised thousands if not millions of eligible voters,” he said in a statement.

The court did not issue a majority opinion, which is often the case with emergency orders.  Justice Brett Kavanaugh issued a concurring opinion saying he believes there is a “fair prospect” the rules fall within the Postal Service’s statutory authority, but that state and local authorities do not have time to implement them before the 2026 elections.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas issued a dissenting opinion saying they believe the government was likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal.
